questions.assertion: A person may choose a job with less pay if it offers regular employment, over a job with high pay but no job security.
questions.reason: Besides more income, people also seek goals such as security, freedom, equal treatment and respect of others.
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: Both are true and R explains A: regular employment enhances a person's sense of security, which is a developmental goal besides income.

questions.assertion: Groundwater is an example of a renewable resource.
questions.reason: Renewable resources are replenished by nature and therefore can never be overused.
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: A is true: groundwater is replenished by nature. R is false: even renewable resources may be overused, as when we use more groundwater than is replenished by rain.

questions.stem: Give two examples from the chapter to show that the developmental goals of two persons or groups can be conflicting.
questions.answer: (1) A girl expects as much freedom and opportunity as her brother, and that he also shares in the household work; her brother may not like this. (2) To get more electricity, industrialists may want more dams, but dams may submerge land and disrupt the lives of people who are displaced, such as tribals, who may prefer small check dams or tanks. So what may be development for one may not be development for the other.
valuePoints: Girl wanting equal freedom and shared housework versus her brother
Industrialists wanting dams versus displaced tribals who prefer small check dams or tanks

rubric.label: First example
rubric.descriptor: A correct example of conflicting goals, with both sides named

rubric.label: Second example
rubric.descriptor: A second, different example with both sides named

questions.stem: What is per capita income? Why is it more useful than total income for comparing countries?
questions.answer: Per capita income (average income) is the total income of the country divided by its total population. Countries have different populations, so comparing total income does not tell us what an average person is likely to earn; average income does.
valuePoints: Per capita income = total income of the country ÷ total population
Countries have different populations, so total income does not show what an average person earns

rubric.label: Meaning
rubric.descriptor: Total income divided by total population

rubric.label: Reason for use
rubric.descriptor: Different populations; average shows what an average person is likely to earn

questions.stem: What does the Infant Mortality Rate indicate? Why does Kerala have a low Infant Mortality Rate?
questions.answer: Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) indicates the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that particular year. Kerala has a low IMR because it has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities.
valuePoints: IMR: children dying before the age of one year per 1000 live births in that year
Kerala has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities

rubric.label: Meaning of IMR
rubric.descriptor: Deaths before age one per 1000 live births in the year

rubric.label: Reason for Kerala
rubric.descriptor: Adequate basic health and educational facilities

questions.stem: 'Money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services that you may need to live well.' Explain this statement with three examples.
questions.answer: Income by itself is not a completely adequate indicator of the goods and services citizens are able to use. (1) Normally money cannot buy you a pollution-free environment. (2) It cannot ensure that you get unadulterated medicines, unless you can afford to shift to a community that already has these things. (3) It may not protect you from infectious diseases unless the whole community takes preventive steps. For many important things the best and cheapest way is collective provision — for example, security for a whole locality, or government schools that make it possible for all children to study.
valuePoints: Money cannot buy a pollution-free environment
Money cannot ensure unadulterated medicines
Money may not protect against infectious diseases unless the whole community takes preventive steps
Collective provision (security, schools) is often the best and cheapest way

rubric.label: First example
rubric.descriptor: Any one valid example from the value points

rubric.label: Second example
rubric.descriptor: A second, different valid example

rubric.label: Third example
rubric.descriptor: A third valid example, or the idea of collective provision explained

questions.stem: Two countries have five citizens each. Monthly incomes (in rupees): Country A — 9500, 10500, 9800, 10000, 10200; Country B — 500, 500, 500, 500, 48000. Calculate the average income of each country. Which country would most people prefer to live in if citizenship were decided by lottery, and what does this show about averages?
questions.answer: Country A: (9500 + 10500 + 9800 + 10000 + 10200) ÷ 5 = 50000 ÷ 5 = Rs 10,000. Country B: (500 × 4 + 48000) ÷ 5 = 50000 ÷ 5 = Rs 10,000. The averages are identical, but most people would prefer Country A because it has a more equitable distribution: people are neither very rich nor extremely poor, whereas in Country B most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich. So while average income is useful for comparison, it does not tell us how income is distributed among people.
valuePoints: Both averages are Rs 10,000
Country A is preferred because income is more equitably distributed
Averages hide disparities: they do not show how income is distributed

rubric.label: Averages
rubric.descriptor: Rs 10,000 for both; ½ mark for each

rubric.label: Preference
rubric.descriptor: Country A, with equitable distribution as the reason

rubric.label: Limitation of averages
rubric.descriptor: Average does not show distribution of income

questions.stem: Why is the issue of sustainability important for development? Explain with the example of groundwater in India.
questions.answer: We would like the level of development to go up further or at least be maintained for future generations, but scientists have warned that the present type and levels of development are not sustainable. Groundwater is under serious threat of overuse in many parts of the country: about 300 districts have reported a water level decline of over 4 metres during the past 20 years, and nearly one-third of the country is overusing its groundwater reserves. In another 25 years, 60 per cent of the country would be doing the same if the present way of using this resource continues. Groundwater is renewable, but if we use more than is replenished by rain we overuse it.
valuePoints: Development should be maintained for future generations; present levels are not sustainable
About 300 districts report water level decline of over 4 metres in the past 20 years; nearly one-third of the country overuses groundwater
Using more than is replenished by rain is overuse; 60 per cent could be overusing in 25 years

rubric.label: Meaning of sustainability
rubric.descriptor: Development maintained for future generations

rubric.label: Groundwater evidence
rubric.descriptor: Any one correct figure from the chapter

rubric.label: Overuse explained
rubric.descriptor: Using more than is replenished by rain, or the 25-year projection

questions.stem: Haryana has a higher per capita income than Kerala, yet Kerala does better on several other indicators. Using data from the chapter, explain why per capita income alone is not an adequate indicator of development.
questions.answer: Per capita income for 2023–24 was Rs 3,25,759 in Haryana and Rs 2,81,001 in Kerala, so by income Haryana is ahead. But Kerala's Infant Mortality Rate is 6 per 1000 live births against 28 in Haryana — nearly three times more in Haryana. Kerala's literacy rate is 94% against Haryana's 82%, and its net attendance ratio at secondary stage is 94 against 73. The reason is that money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services needed to live well. Many important things are best and most cheaply provided collectively, such as health and education facilities. Kerala has a low IMR because it has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities. Hence income must be used along with health and education indicators to measure development.
valuePoints: Haryana's per capita income (Rs 3,25,759) is higher than Kerala's (Rs 2,81,001)
Kerala's IMR is 6 against Haryana's 28
Kerala's literacy (94%) and attendance ratio (94) are higher than Haryana's (82%, 73)
Money cannot buy everything; some goods and services are best provided collectively
Kerala has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities

rubric.label: Income comparison
rubric.descriptor: Haryana's higher per capita income stated with figures

rubric.label: IMR comparison
rubric.descriptor: Kerala 6 versus Haryana 28

rubric.label: Education comparison
rubric.descriptor: Literacy or attendance ratio compared correctly

rubric.label: Why income is inadequate
rubric.descriptor: Money cannot buy all goods and services; collective provision

rubric.label: Conclusion
rubric.descriptor: Public health and education facilities explain Kerala's performance; income should be used with other indicators

questions.stem: How is the criterion used by the UNDP's Human Development Report for measuring development different from the one used by the World Bank? Illustrate with the data given in the chapter for India and Sri Lanka.
questions.answer: The World Bank's World Development Reports classify countries by per capita income: countries with per capita income of US$ 66,500 per annum and above in 2024 are called high income or rich countries, and those with about US$ 2,300 or less are low-income countries. The Human Development Report published by UNDP compares countries on the educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income. For 2023, Sri Lanka had a Gross National Income per capita of 12,616 (2021 PPP $), life expectancy at birth of 77.5 years and mean years of schooling of 10.8, with an HDI rank of 89. India had 9,047, 72 years and 6.9 years, with an HDI rank of 130. So a small neighbour, Sri Lanka, is ahead of India in every respect. By prefixing 'Human' to development, the report makes clear that what matters is what is happening to the citizens — their health and well-being.
valuePoints: World Bank uses per capita income alone (high income: US$ 66,500 and above in 2024; low income: about US$ 2,300 or less)
UNDP uses education, health and per capita income
Sri Lanka: GNI per capita 12,616, life expectancy 77.5, mean schooling 10.8, HDI rank 89
India: 9,047, 72, 6.9, HDI rank 130
Human development puts people's health and well-being first

rubric.label: World Bank criterion
rubric.descriptor: Per capita income, with the classification

rubric.label: UNDP criterion
rubric.descriptor: Education, health and per capita income

rubric.label: Sri Lanka data
rubric.descriptor: At least two correct figures for Sri Lanka

rubric.label: India data
rubric.descriptor: At least two correct figures for India

rubric.label: Inference
rubric.descriptor: Sri Lanka ahead in every respect; people's well-being is what matters

questions.passage: A study group compared three Indian states using data from their Economics textbook. The Infant Mortality Rate per 1,000 live births (2020) was 28 in Haryana, 6 in Kerala and 27 in Bihar. The literacy rate (2017–18) was 82% in Haryana, 94% in Kerala and 62% in Bihar. The net attendance ratio at the secondary stage for children aged 15–17 years (2017–18) was 73 in Haryana, 94 in Kerala and 69 in Bihar. The group noted that the per capita income of Haryana was the highest of the three states and that of Bihar the lowest.

parts.prompt: Which state has the lowest Infant Mortality Rate?
parts.answer: (b) Kerala — 6 per 1,000 live births, against 28 in Haryana and 27 in Bihar.

parts.prompt: What does the literacy rate measure?
parts.answer: The proportion of literate population in the 7-and-above age group.

parts.prompt: What does Bihar's net attendance ratio of 69 tell us, and why does it matter for development?
parts.answer: About one-third of the children aged 15–17 years in Bihar are not attending school in secondary classes (1 mark). Those who could have been in school are not there, so an indicator like this shows a gap in development that per capita income does not reveal (1 mark).

questions.assertion: Cotton is a product of the primary sector, while cloth is a product of the secondary sector.
questions.reason: Tertiary sector activities, by themselves, do not produce a good but are an aid or a support for the production process.
questions.answer: b
questions.explanation: Both are true, but R describes the tertiary sector and does not explain why cotton is primary (a natural product) and cloth secondary (a manufactured product).

questions.assertion: In India, the shift in the share of the three sectors in GVA has been matched by a similar shift in employment.
questions.reason: Not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors.
questions.answer: d
questions.explanation: A is false: a similar shift has not taken place in employment, and the primary sector continues to be the largest employer. R is true, and is in fact why the shift did not happen.

questions.stem: Why are only final goods and services counted while calculating GDP? Explain with the example of wheat, flour and biscuits.
questions.answer: The value of final goods already includes the value of all the intermediate goods used in making them. A farmer sells wheat to a flour mill, the mill sells flour to a biscuit company for Rs 25 per kg, and the company sells biscuits to consumers for Rs 80. The Rs 80 already includes the value of the flour. Counting wheat and flour separately would count the value of the same things a number of times.
valuePoints: Value of final goods includes the value of intermediate goods
Counting wheat and flour separately would count the same value several times

rubric.label: Reason
rubric.descriptor: Final goods already include intermediate goods; avoids counting the same value many times

rubric.label: Example
rubric.descriptor: Wheat → flour → biscuits used correctly

questions.stem: Distinguish between the public sector and the private sector, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: In the public sector the government owns most of the assets and provides all the services, and its purpose is not just to earn profits — for example, Railways or the post office. In the private sector ownership of assets and delivery of services is in the hands of private individuals or companies, guided by the motive to earn profits — for example, Tata Iron and Steel Company Limited (TISCO) or Reliance Industries Limited (RIL).
valuePoints: Public sector: government owns assets; not just profit; e.g. Railways or post office
Private sector: private individuals or companies own assets; profit motive; e.g. TISCO or RIL

rubric.label: Public sector
rubric.descriptor: Government ownership with a correct example

rubric.label: Private sector
rubric.descriptor: Private ownership, profit motive, with a correct example

questions.stem: What is disguised unemployment? Give one example from an urban area.
questions.answer: Disguised unemployment is underemployment that is hidden: people are apparently working but all of them are made to work less than their potential, so even if some move out, production is not affected. In urban areas, thousands of casual workers such as painters, plumbers and repair persons search for daily work and many do not find it every day; street vendors may spend the whole day pushing a cart but earn very little because they have no better opportunities.
valuePoints: People appear to be working but work less than their potential; hidden unemployment
Urban example: casual workers such as painters or plumbers, or street vendors

rubric.label: Meaning
rubric.descriptor: Working less than potential; hidden, not visible

rubric.label: Urban example
rubric.descriptor: A correct urban example

questions.stem: Give three reasons why the tertiary sector has become so important in India.
questions.answer: (1) Basic services such as hospitals, educational institutions, post and telegraph, police stations, courts, municipal corporations, defence, transport, banks and insurance are required in any country, and in a developing country the government has to provide them. (2) The development of agriculture and industry leads to the development of services such as transport, trade and storage. (3) As income levels rise, some sections of people demand more services like eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals and private schools. (4) New services based on information and communication technology have become important and essential.
valuePoints: Basic services are required and the government has to provide them
Growth of primary and secondary sectors raises demand for transport, trade and storage
Rising incomes increase demand for services like eating out, tourism, private schools
New ICT-based services have grown rapidly

rubric.descriptor: Any one reason from the value points, explained

rubric.descriptor: A second, different reason

rubric.descriptor: A third, different reason

questions.stem: Compare the conditions of employment in the organised and unorganised sectors on any three points.
questions.answer: (1) Registration and rules: organised sector enterprises are registered by the government and follow laws such as the Factories Act and Minimum Wages Act; unorganised sector units are small, scattered and largely outside government control, and rules are not followed. (2) Security: organised sector workers enjoy security of employment; in the unorganised sector employment is not secure and people can be asked to leave without any reason. (3) Hours and benefits: organised sector workers work fixed hours, are paid overtime, and get paid leave, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits and pensions; the unorganised sector has no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays or leave due to sickness, and jobs are low-paid and often not regular.
valuePoints: Registered and following laws versus outside government control
Security of employment versus no job security
Fixed hours, overtime and benefits versus none

rubric.label: First point
rubric.descriptor: Both sectors contrasted on one point

rubric.label: Second point
rubric.descriptor: Both sectors contrasted on a second point

rubric.label: Third point
rubric.descriptor: Both sectors contrasted on a third point

questions.stem: What was the objective of MGNREGA 2005? State its main provisions.
questions.answer: MGNREGA 2005 (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) was a quick measure for the short term that implemented the Right to Work in about 625 districts of India. All those who were able to, and in need of, work in rural areas were guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year by the government. If the government failed to provide employment, it would give unemployment allowances. Work that would in future help to increase production from land was given preference. In 2025 the Act was replaced by Viksit Bharat-G RAM G 2025.
valuePoints: Implemented the Right to Work in about 625 districts as a short-term measure
Guaranteed 100 days of employment a year to those able to and in need of work in rural areas
Unemployment allowance if work not provided; preference to work that raises production from land

rubric.label: Objective
rubric.descriptor: Right to Work / guaranteed employment in rural areas

rubric.label: 100 days
rubric.descriptor: 100 days of employment in a year

rubric.label: Other provision
rubric.descriptor: Unemployment allowance, or preference to work that raises production from land

questions.stem: Laxmi, a small farmer with two hectares of unirrigated land, has all five members of her family working on it. Explain the problem her family faces and suggest ways in which more employment can be created in rural areas.
questions.answer: Laxmi's family faces underemployment (disguised unemployment): everyone works, but no one is fully employed, and two members could move out without affecting production. Ways to create employment: (1) The government can spend money, or banks can give a loan, to construct a well; she can then take a second crop, wheat, in the rabi season, employing two more members. A dam and canals would generate much more employment in agriculture. (2) Government investment in transport and storage, and better rural roads, would let farmers sell their crops and create work in transport and trade. (3) Cheap agricultural credit from banks at a reasonable rate of interest would let farmers buy seeds, fertilisers and pumpsets in time instead of borrowing from moneylenders at high interest. (4) Industries and services can be located in semi-rural areas — a dal mill to process arhar and chickpea, a cold storage for potatoes and onions, honey collection centres near forests, and units processing vegetables and farm produce.
valuePoints: Identifies underemployment / disguised unemployment
Irrigation: a well, dams and canals, allowing a second crop
Investment in transport, storage and rural roads
Cheap credit from banks
Agro-based industries in semi-rural areas: dal mill, cold storage, honey collection

rubric.label: Problem identified
rubric.descriptor: Disguised unemployment explained

rubric.label: Irrigation
rubric.descriptor: Well, dam or canals and a second crop

rubric.label: Transport and storage
rubric.descriptor: Roads, transport or storage creating work

rubric.label: Credit
rubric.descriptor: Cheap credit from banks

rubric.label: Semi-rural industries
rubric.descriptor: At least one example such as a dal mill or cold storage

questions.stem: Why does the government have to provide or support certain activities that the private sector will not provide at a reasonable cost? Explain with examples.
questions.answer: (1) Some things need spending large sums of money, beyond the capacity of the private sector, and collecting money from thousands of users is not easy; even if provided, private firms would charge a high rate — roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity, irrigation through dams. (2) Some activities need government support: selling electricity at the cost of generation may push up costs and force small-scale units to shut down, so the government supplies electricity at affordable rates and bears part of the cost. (3) The government buys wheat and rice from farmers at a 'fair price', stores them in godowns and sells them at a lower price through ration shops, supporting both farmers and consumers. (4) Providing health and education for all, especially elementary education, is the government's duty. (5) It must attend to safe drinking water, housing for the poor, food and nutrition, and the poorest regions — for instance the infant mortality rate of Odisha (36) or Madhya Pradesh (43) is higher than some of the poorest regions of the world.
valuePoints: Heavy spending beyond private capacity: roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity, dams
Electricity at affordable rates for small-scale units
Buying grain at a fair price and selling through ration shops
Health and education for all is the government's duty
Drinking water, housing, nutrition and the poorest regions

rubric.label: Heavy investment
rubric.descriptor: Large spending beyond private capacity, with examples

rubric.label: Supporting industry
rubric.descriptor: Electricity at affordable rates

rubric.label: Supporting farmers and consumers
rubric.descriptor: Fair price purchase and ration shops

rubric.label: Health and education
rubric.descriptor: Government's duty to provide them

rubric.label: Human development
rubric.descriptor: Drinking water, housing, nutrition or poorest regions

questions.passage: The table below gives the estimated number of workers in India in the organised and unorganised sectors in the late 1990s (in millions). Primary sector: organised 1, unorganised 232. Secondary sector: organised 41, unorganised 74, total 115. Tertiary sector: organised 40, unorganised 88, total 128. The total number of workers in the organised sector was 82 million. Many organised sector enterprises are also found in the unorganised sector, and since the 1990s many workers have lost their jobs in the organised sector.

parts.prompt: What was the total number of workers in the primary sector?
Roughly what percentage of workers in the primary sector were in the unorganised sector?
parts.answer: 232 of 233 million, about 99.6 per cent — almost all of them.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage of all workers in India who were in the unorganised sector, and state one reason why they need protection.
parts.answer: Unorganised = 232 + 74 + 88 = 394 million out of a total of 233 + 115 + 128 = 476 million, about 82.8 per cent (1 mark). They need protection because their jobs are low-paid, irregular and not secure, with no paid leave or other benefits, and they are often exploited (1 mark).

questions.assertion: Under barter, a shoe manufacturer who wants wheat must look for a wheat-growing farmer who also wants to buy shoes.
questions.reason: In a barter system, double coincidence of wants is an essential feature.
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: Both are true and R explains A: in barter, what one person desires to sell must be exactly what the other wishes to buy.

questions.assertion: Self Help Groups help poor borrowers overcome the problem of lack of collateral.
questions.reason: Banks lend to Self Help Groups because each member offers land as collateral.
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: banks lend to SHGs, even though members have no collateral as such, because the group is responsible for repayment and follows up any non-repayment seriously.

questions.stem: Modern currency is without any use of its own. Why, then, is it accepted as a medium of exchange?
questions.answer: It is accepted because it is authorised by the government of the country. In India the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, and the law legalises the use of the rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India.
valuePoints: Currency is authorised by the government; RBI issues notes on behalf of the central government
The law says the rupee cannot be refused in settling transactions

rubric.label: Legal tender
rubric.descriptor: No one can legally refuse payment in rupees

questions.stem: Why are demand deposits considered money?
questions.answer: Deposits in bank accounts can be withdrawn on demand. The facility of cheques against demand deposits makes it possible to settle payments directly without cash, as when M. Salim pays the leather supplier by cheque. Since demand deposits are accepted widely as a means of payment, along with currency, they constitute money in the modern economy.
valuePoints: Deposits can be withdrawn on demand
Cheques against them settle payments without cash; widely accepted as a means of payment

questions.stem: What is collateral? Why do lenders ask for it?
questions.answer: Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns — such as land, building, vehicle, livestock or deposits with banks — and uses as a guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid. Lenders ask for it because if the borrower fails to repay, the lender has the right to sell the asset to obtain payment.
valuePoints: An asset owned by the borrower used as a guarantee, e.g. land, livestock, bank deposits
If the loan is not repaid, the lender can sell it to obtain payment

rubric.label: Meaning with example
rubric.descriptor: Asset used as guarantee, with an example

rubric.label: Why lenders ask
rubric.descriptor: Right to sell it if the loan is not repaid

questions.stem: How do banks mediate between those who have surplus funds and those who need funds?
questions.answer: Banks accept deposits from the public and pay interest on them. They keep only a small proportion as cash — banks in India hold about 5 per cent of their deposits as cash — to pay depositors who come to withdraw on any given day. They use the major portion of the deposits to extend loans to borrowers. Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on deposits, and the difference is their main source of income.
valuePoints: Accept deposits and pay interest
Keep about 5 per cent as cash; lend the major portion
Charge higher interest on loans than on deposits; the difference is their income

rubric.descriptor: Accept deposits from people with surplus funds

rubric.label: Loans
rubric.descriptor: Keep a small cash reserve and lend the major portion

rubric.label: Interest difference
rubric.descriptor: Higher interest on loans; difference is the main income

questions.stem: Credit can help a borrower in one situation and trap a borrower in another. Explain with the examples of Salim and Swapna.
questions.answer: Salim, a shoe manufacturer, received an order for 3,000 pairs of shoes. He took credit from the leather supplier and an advance from the large trader to meet working capital needs, completed production on time, made a good profit and repaid the loans — credit increased his earnings. Swapna, a small farmer, borrowed from a moneylender to grow groundnut; her crop was hit by pests and failed, the debt grew, and she had to sell part of her land — a debt trap. Whether credit is useful therefore depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is some support in case of loss.
valuePoints: Salim used credit for working capital, delivered the order and repaid with profit
Swapna's crop failed; the debt grew and she sold part of her land (debt trap)
Usefulness depends on the risks and whether there is support in case of loss

rubric.label: Salim
rubric.descriptor: How credit raised his earnings

rubric.label: Swapna
rubric.descriptor: Crop failure leading to a debt trap

rubric.label: Conclusion
rubric.descriptor: Depends on risk and support in case of loss

questions.stem: Distinguish between formal and informal sources of credit on any three points.
questions.answer: (1) Lenders: formal loans come from banks and cooperatives; informal lenders include moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends. (2) Supervision: the Reserve Bank of India supervises the formal sources; no organisation supervises informal lenders, who can use unfair means to get their money back. (3) Interest: most informal lenders charge a much higher interest than formal lenders, so the cost of borrowing is much higher. (4) Collateral: banks require documents and collateral, whereas moneylenders, who know borrowers personally, often lend without collateral.
valuePoints: Banks and cooperatives versus moneylenders, traders, relatives
RBI supervision versus no supervision
Lower versus much higher interest
Documents and collateral versus often no collateral

rubric.label: First point
rubric.descriptor: Both sources contrasted on one point

rubric.label: Second point
rubric.descriptor: Both sources contrasted on a second point

rubric.label: Third point
rubric.descriptor: Both sources contrasted on a third point

questions.stem: What are Self Help Groups? Explain how they work and why they are important for the rural poor, especially women.
questions.answer: SHGs organise the rural poor, in particular women, into small groups and pool their savings. A typical SHG has 15–20 members, usually from one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly; saving per member varies from Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more. Members take small loans from the group at interest that is still less than the moneylender's. After a year or two of regular saving, the group becomes eligible for a bank loan, sanctioned in the name of the group, to create self-employment — for releasing mortgaged land, working capital, housing materials, or assets like sewing machines, handlooms and cattle. The group decides the purpose, amount, interest and repayment schedule, and is responsible for repayment, so banks lend even without collateral. SHGs help women become financially self-reliant, and their regular meetings are a platform to discuss social issues such as health, nutrition and domestic violence.
valuePoints: 15–20 members pooling savings of Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more
Small loans from the group at less than the moneylender's interest
After a year or two, bank loans in the group's name for self-employment
Group decides and is responsible for repayment, overcoming lack of collateral
Financial self-reliance for women and a platform for social issues

rubric.label: Meaning
rubric.descriptor: Small groups of rural poor, mainly women, pooling savings

rubric.label: Internal lending
rubric.descriptor: Loans from the group at lower interest

rubric.label: Bank linkage
rubric.descriptor: Bank loan in the group's name after regular saving

rubric.label: Collateral problem
rubric.descriptor: Group responsibility replaces collateral

rubric.label: Wider benefits
rubric.descriptor: Self-reliance for women; platform for social issues

questions.stem: What are the terms of credit? Compare the terms of credit faced by Megha, Shyamal and Arun in the chapter.
questions.answer: Interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment together comprise the terms of credit; they vary with the lender and the borrower. Megha took a bank loan of Rs 5 lakhs for a house at 12 per cent per annum, to be repaid in 10 years in monthly instalments; she submitted her employment records and salary documents, and the bank kept the papers of the new house as collateral. Shyamal, with 1.5 acres, earlier borrowed from the village moneylender at five per cent per month (60 per cent per annum) and now borrows from an agricultural trader at three per cent per month, who also makes him promise to sell his crop to the trader. Arun, with seven acres, received a bank loan at 8.5 per cent per annum, repayable anytime in the next three years. So formal loans carry lower interest but require documents and collateral, which the better-off can provide, while informal loans cost far more.

questions.stem: How have improvements in transportation technology stimulated the globalisation process?
questions.answer: The past fifty years have seen several improvements in transportation technology, which have made much faster delivery of goods across long distances possible at lower costs. Goods are placed in containers that can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks; containers have led to a huge reduction in port handling costs and increased the speed with which exports reach markets. The cost of air transport has also fallen, enabling much greater volumes of goods to be transported by airlines.

questions.answer: Technology in telecommunications, computers and the Internet has been changing rapidly. Telecommunication facilities (telegraph, telephone including mobile phones, fax), helped by satellite communication devices, are used to contact one another around the world, access information instantly and communicate from remote areas. Computers have entered almost every field, and the Internet lets us obtain and share information and send instant e-mail and talk across the world at negligible cost. In the example, the text of the magazine is sent through the Internet to the Delhi office; the Delhi designers get orders on the design from London through telecommunication facilities; the designing is done on a computer; after printing the magazines are sent by air to London; and payment from a bank in London to a bank in Delhi is made instantly through e-banking. questions.stem: Explain the role of MNCs, foreign investment and foreign trade in the process of globalisation, with the example of Ford Motors in India.
questions.answer: In the past two to three decades, more and more MNCs have been looking for locations around the world which would be cheap for their production, and foreign investment by MNCs in these countries has been rising. At the same time, foreign trade between countries has been rising rapidly, and a large part of it is controlled by MNCs. For instance, the Ford Motors car plant in India not only produces cars for Indian markets, it also exports cars to other developing countries and car components for its many factories around the world. Activities of most MNCs thus involve substantial trade in goods and services. The result of greater foreign investment and greater foreign trade has been greater integration of production and markets across countries — globalisation. More goods, services, investments and technology are moving between countries, and most regions of the world are in closer contact than a few decades back.

parts.prompt: Why did the Indian government put barriers on foreign trade and investment after Independence?
parts.answer: To protect producers within the country from foreign competition, since industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s.

questions.stem: What factors gave birth to the consumer movement in India? Trace its evolution.
questions.answer: The consumer movement arose out of dissatisfaction of consumers with unfair practices by sellers, when no legal system was available to protect them. Rampant food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration of food and edible oil gave birth to the movement in an organised form in the 1960s. Till the 1970s, consumer organisations were largely engaged in writing articles and holding exhibitions, and formed groups to look into malpractices in ration shops and overcrowding in road passenger transport. The movement put pressure on business and government, and in 1986 the government enacted the Consumer Protection Act (COPRA), amended in 2019. More recently India has seen an upsurge in the number of consumer groups.

questions.stem: Explain the right to safety with the help of the case of Reji Mathew.
questions.answer: Reji Mathew, a Class IX student, was operated on for removal of tonsils in a private clinic in Kerala; due to improper anaesthesia he was crippled for life. His father claimed compensation of Rs 5,00,000 for medical negligence in the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, which dismissed it for insufficient evidence. On appeal, the National Commission held the hospital responsible for medical negligence and directed it to pay the compensation. Consumers have the right to be protected against the marketing of goods and delivery of services that are hazardous to life and property, and producers must strictly follow safety rules — for example, the safety valve of a pressure cooker must be of high quality.

questions.stem: Describe the three-tier system set up under COPRA for the redressal of consumer disputes.
questions.answer: COPRA set up a three-tier quasi-judicial machinery at the district, state and national levels. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission deals with cases involving claims up to Rs 1 crore. The State Commission deals with claims between Rs 1 crore and Rs 10 crore. The National Commission deals with claims exceeding Rs 10 crore. If a case is dismissed at the district level, the consumer can appeal in the state and then in the national-level commission.
valuePoints: District Commission: claims up to Rs 1 crore
State Commission: between Rs 1 crore and Rs 10 crore
National Commission: above Rs 10 crore; appeals from district to state to national

questions.stem: Critically examine the progress of the consumer movement in India. What changes did the 2019 amendment to COPRA bring?
questions.answer: Progress: India observes 24 December as National Consumers' Day, the day Parliament enacted the Consumer Protection Act in 1986, and it is one of the countries with exclusive authority for consumer redressal. There are more than 2000 consumer groups, though only about 50–60 are well organised and recognised. The enactment of COPRA also led to separate Departments of Consumer Affairs in central and state governments. Problems: the redressal process is becoming cumbersome, expensive and time consuming; consumers often have to engage lawyers; filing and attending proceedings takes time; cash memos are not issued in most purchases, so evidence is hard to gather; and most purchases are small retail sales. Awareness is spreading but slowly, and rules for markets are often not followed. The 2019 amendment included buying through the internet; a service provider or manufacturer responsible for a service deficiency or defective product can be penalised or even imprisoned; and settlement through a neutral mediator is encouraged at all three tiers.
valuePoints: 24 December National Consumers' Day; exclusive redressal authority

Redressal is cumbersome, expensive and slow; lawyers; no cash memos
Awareness spreading slowly; rules often not followed
2019: internet purchases included; penalties or imprisonment; mediation at all three tiers

questions.stem: Explain the consumer's right to information and right to seek redressal, with examples from the chapter.
questions.answer: Right to information: consumers have the right to be informed about the particulars of goods and services — ingredients, price, batch number, dates of manufacture and expiry, address of the manufacturer, directions for use of medicines and washing instructions for garments. They can then seek replacement if a product is defective within the expiry period, and protest if a good is sold above the MRP. The right has been expanded to government services by the RTI Act of October 2005: Amritha, who had no news of her job interview result, filed an RTI application, learnt the reasons for the delay and received her call letter. Right to redressal: consumers can seek redressal against unfair trade practices and exploitation, and get compensation depending on the degree of damage. Prakash's money order did not reach his daughter; after the post office did not respond satisfactorily, he took advice from the local consumer protection council, filed a case in a district Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, and pleaded it himself. Complaints can be filed with or without lawyers, individually or as a group (class action suit), physically or through the internet.

questions.passage: Abirami joined a two-year course at a coaching institute in New Delhi and paid Rs 61,020 as a lump sum for the whole course. At the end of one year she decided to opt out, as the quality of teaching was not up to the mark, but the institute refused to refund the fee for the second year. She filed a case in the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, which directed the institute to refund Rs 28,000. The institute appealed in the State Commission. The State Commission upheld the District Commission's direction, fined the institute Rs 25,000 for a frivolous appeal, and restrained all educational and professional institutions in the state from charging fees for the entire course in advance.

parts.prompt: Which consumer right did the District Commission uphold in Abirami's case?
parts.answer: (b) Right to choice — the Commission said she had the right to choose whether to continue receiving the service.

parts.prompt: Why was the institute fined Rs 25,000?
parts.answer: For filing a frivolous appeal in the State Commission.

parts.prompt: How did the State Commission's order help students beyond Abirami? What does the case show about the consumer redressal system?
parts.answer: It restrained all educational and professional institutions in the state from charging fees for the entire course in advance, so other students are also protected (1 mark). It shows that consumers can get justice through the three-tier commissions, and that a case can move from the district to the state level on appeal (1 mark).
